extracted.intended_audience: journalists, publishers, news organisations, media regulators and policymakers in Council of Europe member states
extracted.subtask_description: Council of Europe resolution enumerating ethical principles and professional standards for journalism, directed at media professionals and organisations across member states. Covers duties to citizens, distinctions between news and opinion, rights to information, editorial rules, conflict situations and self-regulation mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1. Ethical responsibility towards citizens and society
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to the legal rights and obligations set forth in the relevant legal norms, the media have an ethical responsibility towards citizens and society which must be underlined at the present time, when information and communication play a very important role in the formation of citizens' personal attitudes and the development of society and democratic life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises media duties beyond mere legal compliance because of media's strong role in shaping attitudes and democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2. Profession comprises rights and obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The journalist's profession comprises rights and obligations, freedoms and responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames journalism as a profession balancing liberties with responsibilities; both sides are integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3. Clear distinction between news and opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic principle of any ethical consideration of journalism is that a clear distinction must be drawn between news and opinions, making it impossible to confuse them. News is information about facts and data, while opinions convey thoughts, ideas, beliefs or value judgments on the part of media companies, publishers or journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News must be factual; opinions may be subjective but should be clearly labelled and not conflated with factual reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4. News based on truthfulness, verification and impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: News broadcasting should be based on truthfulness, ensured by the appropriate means of verification and proof, and impartiality in presentation, description and narration. Rumour must not be confused with news. News headlines and summaries must reflect as closely as possible the substance of the facts and data presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibits presenting rumours as news; headlines/summaries should accurately reflect substance; verification mechanisms required.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5. Opinions expressed honestly and ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression of opinions may entail thoughts or comments on general ideas or remarks on news relating to actual events. Although opinions are necessarily subjective and therefore cannot and should not be made subject to the criterion of truthfulness, we must ensure that opinions are expressed honestly and ethically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinions need not be fact-true but must be honest and adhere to ethical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: 6. Opinion-comments must not deny or conceal facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions taking the form of comments on events or actions relating to individuals or institutions should not attempt to deny or conceal the reality of the facts or data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinion pieces commenting on factual events must not distort or conceal actual facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7. Media's work as mediation serving citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The media's work is one of "mediation", providing an information service, and the rights which they own in connection with freedom of information depends on its addressees, that is the citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames the media's rights as deriving from serving citizens' information needs; puts citizens at the centre of media purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8. Information as a fundamental right of the citizen
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is a fundamental right which has been highlighted by the case-law of the European Commission and Court of Human Rights ... The owner of the right is the citizen, who also has the related right to demand that the information supplied by journalists be conveyed truthfully, in the case of news, and honestly, in the case of opinions, without outside interference by either the public authorities or the private sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects citizens' entitlement to truthful news and honest opinions; stresses freedom from public or private interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: 9. Public authorities must not consider they own information
rubrics_metrics.description: The public authorities must not consider that they own information. The representativeness of such authorities provides the legal basis for efforts to guarantee and extend pluralism in the media and to ensure that the necessary conditions are created for exercising freedom of expression and the right to information and precluding censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages pluralism and rejects state ownership/control of information; references Committee of Ministers' Declaration on Freedom of Expression and Information.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10. Distinction between publishers, proprietors and journalists; protect freedom within media
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with journalism it must be borne in mind that it relies on the media, which are part of a corporate structure within which a distinction must be made between publishers, proprietors and journalists. To that end, in addition to safeguarding the freedom of the media, freedom within the media must also be protected and internal pressures guarded against.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for protecting internal editorial freedom and guarding against pressures from owners or management.

rubrics_metrics.name: 11. Limit entrepreneurial objectives by access-to-information conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: News organisations must consider themselves as special socio-economic agencies whose entrepreneurial objectives have to be limited by the conditions for providing access to a fundamental right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial aims should not override citizens' right to information; organisations are special agencies with public obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12. Transparency of media ownership and management
rubrics_metrics.description: News organisations must show transparency in matters of media ownership and management, enabling citizens to ascertain clearly the identity of proprietors and the extent of their economic interest in the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires public disclosure of proprietors and their economic interests to allow citizens to judge potential biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 13. Respect publishers' orientations but limit them by truthful reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Inside the news organisation, publishers and journalists must co-exist, bearing in mind that the legitimate respect for publishers' and owners' ideological orientations is limited by the absolute requirements on truthful news reporting and ethical opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners' ideology may be respected, but cannot compromise truthful news or ethical opinion; citizens' right to information is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: 14. Reinforce safeguards on journalists' freedom: conscience clause and source secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: These requirements are such that we must reinforce the safeguards of the journalist's freedom of expression, for they must in the last instance operate as the ultimate sources of information. In this connection we must legally expand and clarify the nature of the conscience clause and professional secrecy vis-à-vis confidential sources, harmonising national provisions on this matter so that they can be implemented in the wider context of democratic Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for legal recognition/clarification of conscience clauses and protection of confidential sources across member states.

rubrics_metrics.name: 15. Neither owners nor journalists own the news; do not exploit news for revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither publishers and proprietors nor journalists should consider that they own the news. News organisations must treat information not as a commodity but as a fundamental right of the citizen. To that end, the media should exploit neither the quality nor the substance of the news or opinions for purposes of boosting readership or audience figures in order to increase advertising revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibits treating news as a commodity or exploiting substance to chase audiences or ad revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: 16. Treat the audience as individuals, not a mass
rubrics_metrics.description: If we are to ensure that information is treated ethically, its target audience must be considered as individuals and not as a mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages respect for individual rights/needs rather than mass-targeted strategies that may dehumanise subjects or audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: 17. Journalism indispensable for democratic participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Information and communication as conveyed by journalism through the media ... has decisive importance for the development of the individual and society. It is indispensable for democratic life, since if democracy is to develop fully it must guarantee citizens participation in public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stresses civic role of journalism in enabling informed participation in public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18. Importance of radio and television news for culture and education
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of information, especially radio and television news, for culture and education was highlighted ... Its effects on public opinion are obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights particular influence of broadcast media on culture, education and opinion; implies higher responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: 19. Media do not represent public opinion or replace public authorities' functions
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be wrong to infer from the importance of this role that the media actually represent public opinion or that they should replace the specific functions of the public authorities or institutions of an educational or cultural character such as schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against treating media as representative bodies or substitutes for educational/public institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 20. Avoid transforming media into authorities ('mediocracy')
rubrics_metrics.description: This would amount to transforming the media and journalism into authorities or counter-authorities ("mediocracy"), even though they would not be representative of the citizens or subject to the same democratic controls as the public authorities, and would not possess the specialist knowledge of the corresponding cultural or educational institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media must not claim authority they do not have; they lack democratic controls and specialist institutional knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: 21. Do not alter truthful, impartial information to shape public opinion; investigative limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Therefore journalism should not alter truthful, impartial information or honest opinions, or exploit them for media purposes, in an attempt to create or shape public opinion, since its legitimacy rests on effective respect for the citizen's fundamental right to information ... Legitimate investigative journalism is limited by the veracity and honesty of information and opinions and is incompatible with journalistic campaigns conducted on the basis of previously adopted positions and special interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibits shaping public opinion via distortion; investigative journalism must remain truthful and not driven by preexisting agendas or special interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: 22. Respect presumption of innocence and refrain from judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: In journalism, information and opinions must respect the presumption of innocence, in particular in cases which are still sub judice, and must refrain from making judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should avoid prejudicial reporting on suspects or cases before courts; maintain non-judgemental language.

rubrics_metrics.name: 23. Right to privacy respected; public office does not remove privacy rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of individuals to privacy must be respected. Persons holding office in public life are entitled to protection for their privacy except in those cases where their private life may have an effect on their public life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance privacy vs public interest: only when private life affects public duties may intrusion be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: 24. Balance Article 8 (privacy) and Article 10 (freedom of expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempt to strike a balance between the right to respect for private life, enshrined in Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and the freedom of expression set forth in Article 10, is well documented in the recent case-law of the European Commission and Court of Human Rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow ECHR case law when reconciling privacy and free expression; use established legal balancing tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: 25. End does not justify the means; obtain information legally and ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: In the journalist's profession the end does not justify the means; therefore information must be obtained by legal and ethical means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbids illegal or unethical newsgathering even for important stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: 26. Correct false or erroneous items speedily and fully; provide remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: At the request of the persons concerned, the news media must correct, automatically and speedily, and with all relevant information provided, any news item or opinion conveyed by them which is false or erroneous. National legislation should provide for appropriate sanctions and, where applicable, compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligation to publish prompt corrections with full information; supports legal remedies and sanctions where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: 27. Implement right of reply and transfrontier television provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to harmonise the application and exercise of this right in the member states of the Council of Europe, we must implement Resolution (74) 26 on the right of reply ... and also the relevant provisions of the European Convention on Transfrontier Television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls member states to implement existing right-of-reply frameworks and related treaty provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 28. Guarantee decent pay and proper working conditions for journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to ensure high-quality work and independence on the part of journalists, they must be guaranteed decent pay and proper working conditions and facilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material conditions and remuneration are essential to professional independence and quality journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: 29. Avoid connivance with public authorities or economic sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: In the relations which the journalist must maintain in the course of his duties with the public authorities or the various economic sectors, care should be taken to avoid any kind of connivance liable to affect the independence and impartiality of journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should maintain distance from authorities and commercial actors to preserve impartiality and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 30. Do not confuse controversial/sensational items with important information; avoid exploiting duties for prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: In journalism, controversial or sensational items must not be confused with subjects on which it is important to provide information. The journalist must not exploit his duties for the principal purpose of acquiring prestige or personal influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise informational importance over sensationalism; avoid self-promotion through editorial work.

rubrics_metrics.name: 31. Require appropriate professional training given complexity and new technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of the complexity of the process of providing information, which is increasingly based on the use of new technologies, speed and conciseness, journalists must be required to have appropriate professional training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports professional education and training to handle fast, technology-driven news processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 32. Rules for editorial staff and editorial boards to regulate relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the newspaper business, publishers, proprietors and journalists must live side by side. To that end, rules must be drawn up for editorial staff in order to regulate professional relations between the journalists and the publishers and proprietors within the media, separately from the normal requirements of labour relations. Such rules might provide for the setting up of editorial boards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests internal codes/rules and editorial boards to manage professional relations and protect editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: 33. Defend democratic values in times of tension; oppose violence and hatred
rubrics_metrics.description: In society, situations of tension and conflict sometimes arise under the pressure of factors such as terrorism, discrimination against minorities, xenophobia or war. In such circumstances the media have a moral obligation to defend democratic values: respect for human dignity, solving problems by peaceful, tolerant means, and consequently to oppose violence and the language of hatred and confrontation and to reject all discrimination based on culture, sex or religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media should proactively promote tolerance, human dignity and non-violence during conflicts and crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: 34. Media must prevent tension and encourage mutual understanding in conflict regions
rubrics_metrics.description: No-one should remain neutral vis-à-vis the defence of democratic values. To that end the media must play a major role in preventing tension and must encourage mutual understanding, tolerance and trust between the various communities in regions where conflict prevails...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages active confidence-building reporting and measures to reduce tensions (example: Secretary General's measures in former Yugoslavia).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35. Protect children and young people from glorifying violence, sexual exploitation and unsuitable language
rubrics_metrics.description: Having regard to the very specific influence of the media, notably television, on the attitudes of children and young people, care must be taken not to broadcast programmes, messages or images glorifying violence, exploiting sex and consumerism or using deliberately unsuitable language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special duty regarding content for children/young audiences; avoid glorification/exploitation and unsuitable language.

rubrics_metrics.name: 36. Media must submit to firm ethical principles guaranteeing freedom and truthful information
rubrics_metrics.description: Having regard to the requisite conditions and basic principles enumerated above, the media must undertake to submit to firm ethical principles guaranteeing freedom of expression and the fundamental right of citizens to receive truthful information and honest opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for media commitment to established ethical principles as foundation for freedom and citizens' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37. Establish self-regulatory bodies comprising publishers, journalists, users and experts
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to supervise the implementation of these principles, self-regulatory bodies or mechanisms must be set up comprising publishers, journalists, media users' associations, experts from the academic world and judges; they will be responsible for issuing resolutions on respect for ethical precepts in journalism, with prior commitment on the part of the media to publish the relevant resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommends multi-stakeholder self-regulation that issues resolutions and requires media to publish them so citizens can judge credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: 38. Publish annual research comparing news with facts as a barometer of credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The self-regulatory bodies or mechanisms, the media users' associations and the relevant university departments could publish each year the research done a posteriori on the truthfulness of the information broadcast by the media, comparing the news with the actual facts. This would serve as a barometer of credibility which citizens could use as a guide to the ethical standard achieved by each medium or each section of the media, or even each individual journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages annual post-publication audits comparing reportage to facts to measure credibility and improve journalistic practice; suggests corrective mechanisms informed by such research.
